orders.description: Plaintiff’s appeal from the February 10, 2014 summary-judgment dismissal.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on a patch of ice in the laundry-room vestibule of defendant’s apartment complex.

legal_issues.finding: Defendant’s general weekly visits, possibly more frequent in cold weather, did not establish the last inspection before the fall. His initial lack-of-constructive-notice showing failed regardless of opposition.

evidence_discussed.description: Defendant’s deposition described only general laundry-room visit practices, not a specific pre-accident inspection.

quality.notes: Apartment-complex ownership is explicit; entrance denotes the laundry-room vestibule. Injured role and accident date are unstated. General visits are not a particular inspection or proof of an established recurring ice condition. The court applies constructive notice; creation and actual notice appear only in the general test. No storm-in-progress finding follows from the presence of ice or mention of cold weather.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is reversed, on the law, with costs, and the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint is denied.
The plaintiff allegedly slipped and fell on a patch of ice located in the vestibule area of the laundry room within an apartment complex owned by the defendant.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Dutchess County (Pagones, J.), dated February 10, 2014, which granted the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

Here, the defendant failed to satisfy his initial burden. The defendant's deposition testimony merely referred to his general practice of going to the laundry room about once a week, or perhaps more in the cold weather.
The defendant tendered no evidence as to when the area in question was last inspected before the time when the plaintiff allegedly fell
As the defendant failed to meet his prima facie burden, it is not necessary to consider the sufficiency of the plaintiff's opposition papers
Accordingly, the Supreme Court should have denied the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

orders.description: Plaintiff’s limited appeal from the May 19, 2014 order granting defendants’ separate dismissal branches.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted the branches of individual unit owners’ motions dismissing the complaint against each.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on a wet linoleum floor in a condominium vestibule and sued individual unit owners. The accident area was a condominium common element.

legal_issues.finding: Individual unit owners established no maintenance duty over the vestibule because it was a common element controlled by the board of managers.
Plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue whether the individual defendants created the wet condition; no creation finding was made.
The dismissal motions were not premature; hope or speculation that further discovery might yield opposing evidence was insufficient.

quality.notes: The actual vestibule is expressly a condominium common element under board control, supporting private premises even though these individual defendants had no maintenance duty. Owner roles refer to their separate units, not ownership/control of the vestibule. Condominium form alone does not specify residential versus commercial use; subtype is unclear. Wetness does not establish liquid composition, and accident date and injured role are unstated. No evidence formats are identified. Caption wording does not override the operative plaintiff-appeal description. One appealed order resolves several motions; all appealed branches are affirmed.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with one bill of costs.

The plaintiff allegedly was injured when she slipped and fell on a wet linoleum floor in the vestibule of a condominium building. She commenced this action against the defendants, who are owners of individual units in the condominium.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the plaintiff appeals, as limited by her brief, from so much of an order of the Supreme Court, Orange County (Sciortino, J.), dated May 19, 2014, as granted those branches of the defendants' separate motions which were for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against each of them.
"[C]ondominium common elements are solely under the control of the board of managers"

Here, the defendants, moving separately, each established their prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law by demonstrating that as individual unit owners of the condominium, they had no duty to maintain the vestibule where the accident occurred, as it was one [*2] of the condominium's common elements
In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact as to, inter alia, whether the defendants created the alleged wet condition that caused the plaintiff to slip and fall

Contrary to the plaintiff's contention, those branches of the defendants' separate motions which were for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against each of them were not premature.
"The mere hope and speculation that evidence sufficient to defeat the motion might be uncovered during discovery is an insufficient basis upon which to deny the motion"
Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly granted those branches of the defendants' separate motions which were for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against each of them.

orders.description: Plaintiff’s appeal from the January 28, 2019 order granting the tenant’s motion and owner’s cross motion.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted New York Atlantic’s motion and McManus-Lorey’s cross motion dismissing the complaint against each.

facts.factual_summary: While delivering flowers to funeral-service premises on March 24, 2014, plaintiff allegedly tripped over the side-entrance door saddle. She had crossed it earlier without incident and described an unobstructed view before her right foot clipped it while she was placing an easel inside.

legal_issues.finding: Defendants established no duty to protect or warn of this readily observable, non-inherently-dangerous door saddle.
The saddle was established to be obvious, readily observable and not inherently dangerous; plaintiff’s prior crossing and unobstructed approach supported that conclusion, with no triable opposition.

evidence_discussed.description: Plaintiff’s deposition described her earlier successful crossing, unobstructed view and right foot striking the saddle during entry with the floral spray/easel.

quality.notes: Express owner and office tenant support private business premises; other premises type denotes funeral/cremation services rather than assuming a religious institution. Delivery activity does not establish an employee or independent-contractor relationship, so injured role remains unclear. Owner and tenant roles belong to different defendants. One order resolves motion and cross motion, both affirmed. The condition was both obvious and non-inherently-dangerous; do not omit the latter or invent comparative-fault/assumption-of-risk holdings. P005 contains only judicial concurrence metadata and is still covered. Apply unchanged rules to this preliminary validation-period case.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed, with one bill of costs.

On March 24, 2014, the plaintiff, while in the process of delivering a large oval-shaped floral arrangement, known as a spray, to the premises owned by the defendant McManus-Lorey Funeral Home, Ltd. (hereinafter McManus-Lorey), allegedly tripped and fell as she stepped over the threshold of the side entrance.

The plaintiff commenced this action against McManus-Lorey and the defendant New York Atlantic Funeral Services Corp. (hereinafter New York Atlantic), which provided cremation services and rented office space at the premises, to recover damages for personal injuries she allegedly sustained.
In an order entered January 28, 2019, the Supreme Court granted the motion and the cross motion. The plaintiff appeals.
New York Atlantic moved for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against it, and McManus-Lorey cross-moved for the same relief as to it.

Here, the defendants established, prima facie, through the plaintiff's deposition testimony, that the condition of the door saddle that allegedly caused the plaintiff to fall was open [*2] and obvious, readily observable by those employing the reasonable use of their senses, and not an inherently dangerous condition

The plaintiff testified that before the accident, she had entered the subject entrance by walking over the door saddle without incident when she delivered a large heart-shaped flower arrangement; that her view was unobstructed when she approached the entrance to re-enter the premises with the spray and an easel upon which the spray would be mounted; and that she had no issue with stepping over the saddle with her left foot, but that her right foot clipped the saddle as she was attempting to place the easel on the floor within the premises as she entered.
Thus, the plaintiff's own testimony established that she was aware of the existence of the door saddle in the entranceway before she fell
In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact.

Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly granted New York Atlantic's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against it and McManus-Lorey's cross motion for the same relief as to it.
"However, there is no duty to protect or warn of conditions that are not inherently dangerous and that are readily observable by the reasonable use of one's senses"

orders.description: Defendant’s appeal from the January 13, 2017 denial of summary judgment.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied defendant landlord’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: After requesting a bathroom in a bodega, plaintiff was directed to the basement and allegedly slipped on water and saturated cardboard there. She observed water leaking near the bathroom doorway after the fall; defendant owned the building and leased a portion to the bodega operators.

legal_issues.finding: Defendant did not establish complete relinquishment of basement possession/control sufficient to avoid liability under the alleged statutory maintenance duty.
The landlord’s out-of-possession defense failed at the initial-burden stage because complete surrender of basement possession and control was not demonstrated.
Plaintiff invoked Administrative Code § 28-301.1; the court found defendant had not established immunity from that duty, not that a violation or liability was conclusively proved.

quality.notes: Building ownership is explicit; retail denotes the bodega and associated basement-bathroom setting, not an assumption about every part of the building. Injured role and accident date are unstated, and requesting a bathroom does not establish a purchase or employment. Water was observed leaking after the fall; no specific pipe or prior notice is supplied. The third-party-action caption does not change that this appeal resolves plaintiff’s substantive claim. No particular evidence format, lease document content or proven retention/violation is invented; failure to establish relinquishment is an initial-burden finding.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.

The plaintiff allegedly was injured when she slipped and fell on water and saturated cardboard on the floor of a basement in a building owned by the defendant. The plaintiff was in a bodega whose owners leased a portion of the building.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the defendant appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Kings County (Carolyn E. Wade, J.), dated January 13, 2017. The order denied the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

The plaintiff asked to use the bathroom and was directed down some stairs at the back of the bodega to a bathroom in the basement. After she fell, the plaintiff saw that there was water leaking from the area of the bathroom doorway.

Here, the plaintiff alleged the violation of a duty imposed by Administrative Code of the City of New York § 28-301.1, which provides that the owner of a building "shall be responsible at all times to maintain the building and its facilities and all other structures regulated by this code in a safe and code-compliant manner"

The defendant failed to meet its prima facie burden of demonstrating that it completely relinquished possession and control of the basement area of the building, such that it cannot be held liable under that Administrative Code provision for injuries caused by a defective condition therein
Accordingly, we agree with the Supreme Court's determination to deny the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint, regardless of the sufficiency of the opposition papers

orders.description: Condominium’s limited appeal from the November 20, 2023 denial of dismissal against it.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied the condominium’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint against it.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on a wet, uncovered portion of the marble lobby floor in her building during a day of snowfall. Staff had placed mats, including an entrance-to-elevator runner, and dry-mopped wet spots; plaintiff had not seen wetness when leaving 15 minutes earlier.

legal_issues.finding: The condominium undertook reasonable maintenance through mats and dry mopping; reasonable care did not require covering every floor area with mats.
The condominium established lack of actual notice of the specific wet condition, with no triable opposition.
Possible recent tracking by entrants and no wetness seen 15 minutes earlier defeated constructive notice; general awareness of snow-related moisture did not establish notice of this condition.
Certified weather reports established an ongoing snowstorm, making the doctrine applicable; plaintiff raised no triable issue against the initial showing.

evidence_discussed.description: Certified weather reports established a snowstorm at the accident time; no accident calendar date or specific measurements are supplied.
Doorman testified to monitoring the lobby throughout the day and mopping wet spots.
Plaintiff admitted seeing no wet floor condition when leaving the building 15 minutes earlier.

quality.notes: Residential lobby and the condominium’s actual staff/mat/mopping operations support private control without inferring title. Other injured role denotes resident, not tenant or unit owner. Manager role captures the condominium’s stated maintenance operations. Accident date is unstated; December 31, 2024 is the decision date within the eligibility window, while the 2025 correction date is not a new decision. Water is the immediate alleged hazard; no exterior ice fall is invented. Potential tracking by plaintiff is not a finding of comparative fault or her creation of the condition. General snow awareness is not a separate recurring-condition holding. Full reversal of the appealed denial and consequential entry of dismissal constitute one disposition and one appealed order. Apply unchanged rules to this preliminary test-period case.

evidence.quote: Order, Supreme Court, New York County (Lori S. Sattler, J.), entered November 20, 2023, which, to the extent appealed from, denied the motion of defendant Two Ten West 77 Condominium (the condominium) for summary judgment dismissing the complaint as against it, unanimously reversed, on the law, without costs, and the motion granted. The Clerk is directed to enter judgment dismissing the complaint as against the condominium.
Plaintiff alleges that she was injured when she slipped and fell on a wet area on the marble floor in the lobby of her building.
At the time of the accident, it had been snowing for most of the day, and building staff had placed mats throughout the lobby, leaving only a small portion of the walkway uncovered.

The condominium established prima facie entitlement to summary judgment by submitting certified weather reports demonstrating that there was an ongoing snowstorm at the time of accident, and that the "storm-in-progress" doctrine therefore applied

The condominium demonstrated that it undertook reasonable maintenance measures to address the wet conditions created by tracked-in snow by laying rubber mats throughout the lobby, including an eight-foot runner from the building entrance to the elevator bank, as well as having the doorman and other staff dry mop any wet spots

Although plaintiff's accident took place on a small portion of the floor that was uncarpeted and remained uncovered, a defendant is not required under the "reasonable care" standard to cover all of its floors with mats to prevent someone from falling on moisture
In response to the condominium's prima facie showing, plaintiff failed to submit evidence sufficient to raise a triable issue of fact.
The condominium also showed lack of actual notice of the specific wet condition that caused plaintiff to slip.

The building's doorman testified that he monitored the condition of the lobby throughout the day and would mop any wet spot, and plaintiff admitted that she did not see any wet condition on the floor when she left the building 15 minutes earlier
Similarly, because the water might have been tracked in by plaintiff or by other residents entering the lobby, there is no basis for a finding of constructive notice

Nor was the condominium's general awareness that the floor might become wet while it was snowing sufficient to establish constructive notice [*2] of the specific condition that caused plaintiff's injury
Plaintiff's opposition did not raise a triable issue of fact regarding notice.
